rationales.A: The map shows towns and trade routes, not a war; large-scale war between settlers and Native peoples came later.
rationales.B: No mass conversion happened in 1612, and the map records places, not baptisms.
rationales.C: The map is crowded with Native towns, peoples, and place names — the Chesapeake world as Native peoples knew it — and Smith could only draw it because Native guides and informants taught him the rivers, villages, and trails. Jamestown survived its first years on Powhatan corn and Native knowledge, not on English self-sufficiency. The royal arms at the center and the English ship in the bay show who the map was for, but the names on the land show who taught Smith what to draw.
rationales.D: The map shows Native towns still standing, not land sold to settlers.
rationales.general:
1. Count what the map is full of. Native towns, Native peoples, Native place names — dozens of them.
2. Ask how Smith learned those names. Background: he had barely explored the region; Native guides and informants taught him.
3. Connect the map to the colony. Background: Jamestown lived on Powhatan corn, and its map lived on Powhatan knowledge.
Remember: a map is evidence too — ask who supplied the knowledge it shows.

stimulus.text: John Smith's map of Virginia, published in 1612 and engraved by William Hole. Native towns and peoples are named across the whole map, and the upper-left inset shows Powhatan enthroned with his courtiers, captioned “Held this state & fashion when Capt. Smith was delivered to him prisoner 1607.” A Native man with a bow stands at the right, and the royal arms of James I sit at the center.
